hero.kicker: Can you predict how much electricity Europe will use tomorrow?
hero.cap: lower average error, in megawatts, than a simple guess.
hero.fine: That is the LightGBM model I trained, forecasting hourly electricity demand in each of 10 European countries, a day ahead. A simple guess repeats what happened at the same hour a week earlier. Tested on 28 days it never saw (2 Sep 2020 to 29 Sep 2020), scored once.

verdict: The model beat the simple guess on 27 of 28 days.
plain: Grid operators publish a day-ahead demand forecast that traders and plant schedulers lean on. I built the same kind of forecast for 10 European countries and tested it honestly. I hid the last 28 days, then made the model forecast each one from the night before. It was off by about 423 MW per country per hour. A simple guess was off by 759. That is 44.3% lower average error, measured in megawatts, and the percentage error is lower in every one of the 10 countries.

I also compared it with the grid operators' own forecast, which was off by 468 MW. In megawatts the difference is small and the 95% range runs from -20 to +94 MW a day, so I cannot say the model is ahead. In percent the model was 0.45 points better (95% range 0.11 to 0.74). Megawatts count the big countries most, percent counts every country the same. The two measures disagree, so my conclusion stands on megawatts, the measure this page leads with: not clearly different.

The operators beat the model in Italy, Spain, Finland, and the model beat them in Germany, France, Poland, Belgium. In Netherlands, Switzerland, Austria the operator forecast is more than 4% away from measured load every year, so those comparisons are not fair. The operators use weather forecasts and my model does not, so weather is the first thing I would add. I did test that on a separate window, in the Weather tab.

compare.base_label: repeat the same hour from a week earlier

findings.lab: lower average error in MW than the simple guess
findings.sub: 423 MW against 759 MW, on 28 days never seen. The model had the lower error on 27 of them.

findings.lab: days with a lower error than the operators' forecast
findings.sub: Not clearly different overall, and the countries split. Average error 423 MW against 468 MW; the model was lower on 19 of 28 days, which is context, not the conclusion.

findings.lab: of actual hours inside the 10% to 90% range
findings.sub: It should be about 80%. The range is a little too narrow, so treat it as optimistic.

steps.sub: Each day, the model sees only data from before that moment and forecasts the next 24 hours for every country.
The real numbers are revealed and the miss is scored. Then the clock moves forward one day.
The simple guess and the operators' forecast are scored on the same hours, by the same code.
The last 28 days were locked away until every choice was frozen. The run is recorded, and a second run is refused. It was scored 1 time(s).

limits: The held-out days are September 2020, right after the spring lockdowns, so demand was not behaving normally. One month of September says little about winter peaks.
The data ends in 2020 and comes from one public source, so this shows the method, not what happens on today's grid.
The main test has no weather input, and the operators' forecasts use weather. A second test on a different window added measured temperature; see the Weather tab.
Holidays are national only. Regional holidays are not in the model.
The operators' forecast was issued about half a day before my forecast and uses information mine does not have. It is a reference line, not a like-for-like opponent.
For Netherlands, Switzerland, Austria the operator series looks like it measures something else, so I report the numbers but do not draw a conclusion from them.
The 10% to 90% range covered 75% of hours against a target of 80%.

The country list was chosen by a rule (complete data, then the largest average load). The rule was changed once after a first development run, and that is written down in the project notes. Countries with the most missing data were not used.
method: Pick a day. At midnight the model may only look at what happened before that moment.
It forecasts every hour of that day, in every country, using demand from the past day, week and four weeks, the hour, weekday, month and national holidays.
Countries differ hugely in size, so the model predicts demand relative to each country's recent level and scales the answer back.
The real numbers are revealed, the miss is scored, and the clock moves forward one day.
A test checks that every feature equals an independent recalculation from raw history, and that a deliberately planted leak is caught.
Choices were made on the 364 development days. The last 28 days were scored once.
glossary: Megawatts, the size of demand in a given hour.
Mean absolute percentage error: the average miss as a share of the real demand. Operators often quote this one.
The average miss divided by the miss of a repeat-last-week guess on the training days. Under 1 means better than that guess.
Days the model never saw while I built it, scored once at the end.
The day-ahead demand forecast that each country's grid operators publish.
data_note: Hourly load and operator forecasts from Open Power System Data (originally the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform), 2015-01-02 to 2020-09-30.

evidence.title: How the holiday 2022 winter storm confounded grid operators' forecast models
evidence.why: A December 2022 winter storm pushed US grid demand past what forecasts predicted, with error rates of up to 9% against the usual target of 3%. In Texas the next-day peak forecast was 67,775 MW and demand came in 8% higher, at 73,658 MW.
evidence.credit: Image: 101cats via Getty Images, via S&P Global

evidence.title: Heat and power: Impacts of the 2025 heatwave in Europe
evidence.why: In the 2025 European heatwave, daily power demand rose by up to 14% in Spain, and average daily prices rose by 106% to 175% in Poland, France and Germany. Demand moves like this are what a day-ahead forecast has to anticipate.
evidence.credit: Image: Martin Bond, Alamy, via Ember

evidence.title: Electricity load forecasting under extreme heat and cold waves
evidence.why: The authors report that load forecasting models trained mostly on ordinary weather often fail in heat and cold waves. Their analysis puts the extra cost of each megawatt-hour under-forecast a day ahead, in one extreme-weather period, at about 449 USD.
evidence.credit: Fig. 1, Lu et al., Nature Communications (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

fleet.intro: An example of how this work could move into a real grid operator or utility. The middle column is a plan, not something I have built.

columns.title: What carries over
items: The backtest harness: forecast each day using only what was known before it, then move forward one day.
The leak test: every feature is checked against an independent recalculation, and a deliberately planted leak is caught.
Simple baselines scored first, so a model has to beat them to count.
Held-out days scored once, with every number on this site read from a results file.
A weather test on a separate window, with the model's settings left alone.

columns.title: What would change
items: Their own meter and control-room data instead of public national totals.
Real weather forecasts, not measured temperature, since that is what is known the night before.
Regional holidays, school terms, and solar and wind generation as inputs.
Smaller areas than whole countries, and a rule for areas with no history.
A forecast range scored on what a wrong forecast costs in balancing, not only on average error.
Monitoring to catch the model drifting after launch.

columns.title: What this does not prove
items: One held-out month and one weather window say little about a full year.
The data is public national load, not a utility's live feeds.
It was never tested against a running system.
The operators' own forecast is issued earlier and uses weather forecasts, so it is a reference, not a like-for-like opponent.

weather.verdict: With measured temperature added, the model missed 14% less than without it.
plain: The first test asked whether the model could match the grid operators. This one asks what weather adds. I gave the same model four extra numbers: the temperature at the hour being forecast, its average over the day, and how far below 15 degrees or above 22 degrees it was. Then I forecast 28 days it had not seen (3 Nov 2018 to 30 Nov 2018), next to the same model without temperature, a simple guess and the operators.

Without weather the model missed by 579 MW per country per hour. With weather it missed by 497 MW, which is 14% lower. It was the better of the two on 20 of 28 days. The 95% range, 40 to 121 MW a day, stays on one side of zero. Against the grid operators' forecast (615 MW) the weather model (497 MW) is ahead, 19% lower in error.

Weather lowered the percentage error in all 10 countries. The temperature the model got is what was measured, not a forecast, so a real system would do worse than this. Read it as the most weather could add to this model, not as a result you could bank.

cards.sub: 579 MW without, 497 MW with, on 28 days.
The 95% range, 40 to 121 MW a day, stays on one side of zero.

caveats: Measured temperature stands in for a weather forecast. Real forecasts are wrong by a degree or two, so this is an upper bound on what weather would give.
One window, 28 days, in autumn heating season. It says nothing about summer cooling or about holidays.
The window was chosen before any weather result existed and sits wholly before the development days used for the first test. It is the only time it was scored.
Settings were the same as the model without weather. Nothing was tuned for the weather version, so a tuned one could do better or worse.
Temperature is a population-weighted country average from NASA's MERRA-2 reanalysis via Open Power System Data. Wind, cloud and sun are not included.
weather.data_note: Weather: Open Power System Data weather_data (MERRA-2 reanalysis, population-weighted country temperature).

mind.title: It beats the simple guess in most countries
mind.detail: It had the lower percentage error in 10 of 10 countries.

mind.title: The result is not just the biggest country
mind.detail: With Germany removed, the model still made 46.8% fewer misses than the simple guess.

mind.title: It wins on most days, not a few lucky ones
mind.detail: It beat the simple guess on 27 of 28 held-out days.

mind.title: It keeps up with the operators where the comparison is fair
mind.detail: It had the lower or equal percentage error than the operators in 4 of 7 countries whose operator series looks sound. The operators have weather forecasts and the model does not.

mind.title: The 10% to 90% range can be trusted
mind.detail: The range caught 75% of held-out hours; an ideal range catches 80%. That is a little too narrow, so treat it as optimistic.

mind.title: Weather helps on days the model was not tuned on
mind.detail: On a separate window, measured temperature cut the miss by 14.2%, and the 95% range on the daily gap stays above zero.

mind.title: It keeps winning in other months and years
mind.detail: Only one held-out month and one weather window were scored, so I cannot rule this out.
